AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: To compare the effects of classic progressive resistance training (PRT) versus eccentric strength-enhanced training (EST) on the performance of functional tests and different strength manifestations in the lower limb of patients with multiple sclerosis (PwMS).

AbstractText.Label: PARTICIPANTS
AbstractText.content: Fifty-Two PwMS (19 men and 33 women) belonging to MS associations from the Castilla y León/Spain.

AbstractText.Label: INTERVENTION
AbstractText.content: Participants were assigned to one of two groups: a control group that performed PRT or an experimental group that performed EST. In both groups, the knee extensor muscles were trained for 12 weeks.

AbstractText.Label: MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES
AbstractText.content: Before and after 12 weeks of training, maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC) and one repetition maximum (1RM) of the knee extensors were evaluated, as were the chair stand test (CST) and timed 8-foot up and go (TUG) functional tests.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: No differences were found between the groups in the initial values for different tests. For intragroup comparisons found significant differences in CST (F= 69.4; p= 0.000), TUG (F=40.0; p=0.000) and 1RM (F=57.8; p=0.000). For intergroup comparisons, EST presented better results than PRT in CST (EST: 4.7±2.8% vs PRT: 1.9±2.8%; F=13.1; p=0.001) and TUG (EST: -2.9±4.7 vs PRT: -0.41±5.6; F=5.6; p=0.022).

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: EST produces similar effects as PRT on the improvement of 1RM, TUG, and CST for PwMS. However, for patients who participated in this study the EST seems to promote a better transfer of strength adaptations to the functional tests, which are closer to daily-living activities.
